evidence_text: ### 3.1 Diagnosis and targets Hypertension is diagnosed when clinic blood pressure is 140/90 mmHg or higher on two visits, or 135/85 mmHg or higher on home monitoring. The treatment target is below 140/90 mmHg for most adults and **below 130/80 mmHg** for patients with diabetes (DIS-001), chronic kidney disease (DIS-003), or established cardiovascular disease.

# DG-01: Cardiovascular Guidelines (Fictional Reference) > **SYNTHETIC DATA NOTICE.** This document is a fictional reference guideline written for software benchmarking and education. Its criteria, thresholds, and algorithms are invented, may differ from real-world practice, and must not be used for clinical decisions. "Reference Guideline" statements are kept separate from "MediCore Policy" statements (time targets and workflow rules owned by the HO documents).

### 4.1 Diagnosis HFrEF requires symptoms or signs of heart failure plus a left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of **40% or lower** on echocardiography (LAB-023). NT-proBNP (LAB-008) supports the diagnosis when above 450 pg/mL under age 50, above 900 pg/mL between 50 and 75, and above 1,800 pg/mL over 75. NT-proBNP is not a stand-alone diagnostic test.

### 4.4 Sick-day rule During vomiting, diarrhea, or poor oral intake the patient should pause the ACE inhibitor, spironolactone, diuretic, and metformin until eating and drinking normally for 24 to 48 hours.

### 3.5 SGLT2 inhibitor precautions SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose. The reference guideline requires: 1. Teach the **sick-day rule** at initiation: stop the drug during vomiting, fever, diarrhea, or poor oral intake, and for 3 days before elective surgery. 2. Check ketones if unwell even when glucose is not high. 3. After an episode of ketoacidosis attributed to an SGLT2 inhibitor, **do not re-challenge** with the drug class (MP-02). PAT-004 (PR-04) developed ketoacidosis on 2025-12-09 after not following the sick-day rule; empagliflozin was permanently stopped and recorded as an adverse drug reaction.

section: 3.4 Metformin and kidney function (rationale for the renal cap)
evidence_text: ### 3.4 Metformin and kidney function (rationale for the renal cap) Metformin is renally cleared; accumulation raises the risk of lactic acidosis. The reference guideline rule is: | eGFR (mL/min/1.73 m2) | Rule | |---|---| | 45 or higher | No reduction required | | **30 to 44** | **Maximum 1,000 mg per day** | | Below 30 | Stop | MediCore applies this rule through PRO-008 and FPA-03 (HO-02); the practical dose tables are in MP-02 and MP-07. During acute illness with dehydration, pause metformin (sick-day rule). Charts showing the rule in action: PR-01 (eGFR 44 on 2025-02-20, dose reduced 2025-03-13) and PR-04 (eGFR 88, no cap).

section: 8.4 ENC-001-07 to ENC-001-09, the metformin adjustment (2025-02-20 to 2025-05-14)
evidence_text: ### 8.4 ENC-001-07 to ENC-001-09, the metformin adjustment (2025-02-20 to 2025-05-14) On 2025-02-20 creatinine was 158 umol/L, eGFR 44. Under PRO-008 (see HO-02), metformin is capped at 1,000 mg/day when eGFR is 30 to 44 (FPA-03). The PharmaSafe system generated a renal-dose advisory, but it was filed in the pharmacist work queue rather than the prescriber inbox. The dose therefore remained 2,000 mg/day for **21 days** until the pharmacist telephone review of 2025-03-13 (ENC-001-08), when the dose was reduced to 500 mg twice daily and the patient was counseled on sick-day rules. At ENC-001-09 (2025-05-14), eGFR 43 with metformin 1,000 mg/day was compliant. Metformin would be stopped if eGFR fell below 30; it has not.

### 6.5 Hospital-onset C. difficile infection (INC-004) Watery diarrhea began on the evening of 2026-03-06 (hospital day 9). A stool specimen for C. difficile toxin/PCR (LAB-024) was sent at 22:10. The positive result was verified at **08:40 on 2026-03-07**. Contact-enteric precautions (PRO-012) were not started until **15:25**, an interval of 6 hours 45 minutes. During this interval the patient used a shared bathroom with one other patient (no secondary case identified on screening). The delay was reported as **INC-004** and reviewed in HO-08. Treatment: oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 hours (MED-019, oral route) from 2026-03-07 for 10 days, last dose 2026-03-16. Diarrhea resolved at 06:00 on 2026-03-12. Under FPA-10 precautions continue until 72 hours after diarrhea resolves, so they ended at 06:00 on 2026-03-15 (HO-06). Discharge occurred on 2026-03-16 at 10:20.

## 4. C. difficile Precautions (FPA-10) 1. **Trigger:** a positive C. difficile result (LAB-024), or three or more unformed stools in 24 hours in a patient at risk, which allows precautions to start before the result. 2. **Start:** immediately on the call from the laboratory (version 2); the ward nurse records the start time. 3. **Duration:** precautions continue until **72 hours after diarrhea has resolved** (formed stool or return to baseline, FPA-10). Discharge or transfer before that time requires the receiving unit to be informed. 4. **Room and toilet:** single room with dedicated toilet or commode; no shared bathroom. 5. **Cleaning:** sporicidal agent daily and at terminal clean. 6. **Antibiotic review:** stewardship (HO-04) reviews the need for the inciting antibiotic. 7. **Treatment:** oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 hours for 10 days (DG-05, MP-04).

### 4.5 After discharge Discharge after a heart-failure admission requires structured follow-up. The MediCore protocol is PRO-016 in HO-07, which sets a telephone call within 48 hours and a clinic visit within 7 days (FPA-06). Patients on warfarin (MED-013) also need an INR check within 72 hours of discharge under PRO-007 (HO-04). PAT-011 (PR-08) shows what happens when these steps fail.

### 3.1 Standard (FPA-06; all versions) For every patient discharged after an admission for heart failure, or with HFrEF (DIS-004) as an active problem: - **Telephone call within 48 hours of discharge** by Care Coordination. - **Clinic visit within 7 days of discharge** at the heart-failure clinic (DEP-003). - INR check within 72 hours if on warfarin (PRO-007).

## 4. C. difficile Precautions (FPA-10) 1. **Trigger:** a positive C. difficile result (LAB-024), or three or more unformed stools in 24 hours in a patient at risk, which allows precautions to start before the result. 2. **Start:** immediately on the call from the laboratory (version 2); the ward nurse records the start time. 3. **Duration:** precautions continue until **72 hours after diarrhea has resolved** (formed stool or return to baseline, FPA-10). Discharge or transfer before that time requires the receiving unit to be informed. 4. **Room and toilet:** single room with dedicated toilet or commode; no shared bathroom. 5. **Cleaning:** sporicidal agent daily and at terminal clean. 6. **Antibiotic review:** stewardship (HO-04) reviews the need for the inciting antibiotic. 7. **Treatment:** oral vancomycin 125 mg every 6 hours for 10 days (DG-05, MP-04).

### 6.2 DKA insulin infusion transition (FPA-12) 1. Infusion of MED-003 at 0.1 units/kg/hour begins after the potassium rule in DG-02 is satisfied. 2. Beta-hydroxybutyrate (LAB-028) and glucose are checked hourly at first, then every 2 hours. 3. **Transition to subcutaneous insulin is permitted when beta-hydroxybutyrate is below 0.6 mmol/L on two consecutive checks.** 4. Give the first subcutaneous basal dose (MED-002) at least **2 hours before** the infusion is stopped. 5. Example: PAT-004 had values of 0.5 mmol/L at 14:00 and 0.4 at 16:00 on 2025-12-10, so the criterion was met at 16:00; glargine was given at 16:30 and the infusion stopped at 18:30 (PR-04, LD-03).

### 4.3 Resolution criterion The reference guideline defines resolution of ketoacidosis as beta-hydroxybutyrate below 0.6 mmol/L. MediCore requires this on **two consecutive checks** before transition (MediCore Policy, FPA-12, PRO-010, HO-02), and defines its hypoglycemia alert at a glucose below 4.0 mmol/L (72 mg/dL).

PAT-007 (anaphylaxis) must avoid ceftriaxone until allergy evaluation.

### 3.1 Allergy flag before the event At registration in 2024-09 the patient reported a childhood rash to a penicillin. It was entered in the allergy field as "Penicillins: rash, patient-reported, unverified." The low severity and "unverified" status led staff to treat the flag as low risk.

### 4.1 Allergy record Each flag records allergen class (ALG-001 to ALG-006), reaction, severity, date, **verification status**, and source. An **unverified or patient-reported flag is treated as the worst credible reaction** until verified (MP-07). The allergy is updated the same day after any event.

### 5.4 Allergy documentation An allergy entry without verification, such as "rash, patient-reported, unverified," must not be treated as low risk. Before the first dose of a beta-lactam in any patient with an allergy flag, MediCore requires **dual verification** by pharmacist and nurse (PRO-003, FPA-09, HO-02). The failure of this step is the subject of INC-001 (HO-08).

## 5. PRO-008: Renal Dose Adjustment (version 3, effective 2026-05-01) 1. Every inpatient order and every outpatient prescription for a drug in the MP-07 section 4.2 list is checked against the **most recent eGFR**. Pharmacy owns the check; Nephrology (DEP-005) advises. 2. **Metformin (FPA-03):** eGFR 45 or higher no cap; **eGFR 30 to 44 maximum 1,000 mg/day; eGFR below 30 stop** (MP-02, MP-07). 3. Other renal rules follow MP-07, including piperacillin-tazobactam (**3.375 g every 6 hours at eGFR 30 or below**), enoxaparin, lisinopril, spironolactone and apixaban. 4. A new eGFR that falls into a lower band triggers a **renal-dose alert**. In version 1 (to 2025-04-30) the alert went only to the pharmacist work queue; in **version 2 (2025-05-01 to 2026-04-30)** it also went to the prescriber's inbox; in **version 3 (from 2026-05-01)** it does both and in addition: - An **NSAID order (for example MED-026) at eGFR below 60 is a hard stop**; override requires a second pharmacist and a documented reason. 5. The metformin cap should be implemented within **14 days** of the qualifying eGFR. (PAT-001's cap was applied 21 days after the eGFR of 2025-02-20, during version 1 of this protocol, which routed the alert only to the pharmacist queue; PR-01.) 6. The change to version 3 followed INC-005 (PAT-009, ibuprofen prescribed 2026-03-05 with an overridden alert; PR-07, HO-08).

section: 4.3 When an NSAID must not be used
evidence_text: ### 4.3 When an NSAID must not be used Avoid oral NSAIDs in: chronic kidney disease or AKI (DG-03); anticoagulant therapy (DG-06); a history of gastrointestinal bleeding (DG-07); concurrent SSRI plus antiplatelet (section 3); heart failure; NSAID/aspirin hypersensitivity (ALG-003, MP-07). Where any applies, remain at step 2. PAT-009 (CKD G3b) was prescribed ibuprofen against this rule and developed AKI (INC-005, PR-07). PAT-006 (anticoagulated) used acetaminophen (PR-06). PAT-010 developed a bleed on ibuprofen with aspirin and sertraline (PR-07).

### 3.4 Readmission, 2026-02-02 to 2026-02-08 (ENC-011-02) Returned 16 days after discharge with dyspnea and weight 80.1 kg (4.1 kg above dry weight). NT-proBNP 5,300 pg/mL. INR **3.4**, above the 2.0 to 3.0 target. Warfarin was reduced from 4 mg to 3.5 mg daily and an INR recheck was set for 2026-02-05 (3 days), when INR was 2.8. Diuresis resumed; furosemide 40 mg twice daily continued; spironolactone continued (K 4.6). The patient reported a high-salt diet and missing two metoprolol doses per week. Discharged **2026-02-08 at 11:00** with all three obligations met: call completed 2026-02-09 at 09:30 (22 hours 30 minutes), INR 2.6 on 2026-02-10, clinic visit 2026-02-12 (4 days). The case is the principal example of a missed heart-failure follow-up in this dataset; PAT-001 (PR-01) in contrast completed all follow-up on time.

## 2. Purpose and Scope This casebook holds four patients: a heart-failure readmission with a missed follow-up call in a man on warfarin (PAT-011, INC-006), a non-severe pneumonia treated with a short, stewardship-guided course (PAT-012), urosepsis with acute kidney injury and pharmacy-managed vancomycin (PAT-013), and iron-deficiency anemia complicated by a levothyroxine absorption problem (PAT-014). Facts are specific to each patient; several features deliberately resemble charts in PR-01, PR-03, PR-06 and PR-07 and must not be confused with them. Laboratory values are given inline unless a separate report is cited.

### 4.1 MediCore Heart-Failure Readmission Risk Score (fictional) One point each: admission for heart failure in the past 12 months; eGFR below 45; NT-proBNP above the age-band threshold at discharge (DG-01); atrial fibrillation; living alone; unreliable telephone contact. A score of **3 or more** triggers a nurse home-visit offer. PAT-011 scored 3 at the first discharge (atrial fibrillation, NT-proBNP 4,820 pg/mL, prior recent admission), which did not trigger an outreach because the score field was not completed.

### 3.3 Outcome and follow-up The patient stayed 24 hours in the ICU, then on a ward. She was discharged on 2026-05-19 with an epinephrine auto-injector prescription (MED-029) and a revised allergy entry: **ALG-001, anaphylaxis, confirmed 2026-05-17**; cephalosporin cross-reactivity cautions were added per MP-07. Allergy clinic referral was made. Spirometry (LAB-019) on 2026-06-23 (LD-08): FEV1 82% of predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.78, bronchodilator reversibility 14%, supporting well-controlled asthma. The event was reported as **INC-001**; the review, the change to PRO-003 (a hard stop on override of the dual-verification step for beta-lactams, effective 2026-07-01), and the audit findings are in HO-08. Contrast this case with PAT-012 in PR-08, who tolerated the same antibiotic and has no allergy flag.

### 3.5 De-escalation Review at 48 to 72 hours. When susceptibilities are known, narrow to the most selective effective agent and stop vancomycin if no resistant gram-positive organism is isolated. PAT-003 was de-escalated within 5 hours of the susceptibility report (PR-03); PAT-013 had vancomycin stopped at 48 hours (PR-08).

### 4.3 Causes and nephrotoxin avoidance Evaluate prerenal causes (volume depletion), renal causes (nephrotoxins, sepsis), and post-renal obstruction. Key nephrotoxin hazards in this dataset: - **NSAIDs with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic**, the "triple combination," in a patient with CKD (PAT-009). - **Vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam** (MP-06, MP-04), requiring pharmacy-managed dosing and early level checks (PAT-013). - Dehydration during infection, with diuretics and ACE inhibitors continued.

### 3.4 Interactions Ferrous sulfate reduces levothyroxine (MED-024) absorption: separate by **at least 4 hours** (MediCore Policy FPA-14; MP-02, MP-06). PAT-014 illustrates the TSH rise after co-administration (PR-08).

### 6.4 Interpreting TSH Acute illness can transiently alter TSH; avoid dose changes on a single value during illness (PAT-004: TSH 4.1 mIU/L during ketoacidosis, 3.8 on 2026-03-18). Persistent elevation after a new co-medication suggests an absorption problem rather than disease progression (PAT-014: TSH 2.4, then 8.9 after iron was taken 30 minutes after levothyroxine, then 3.2 after separation; PR-08).

section: 4.3 When an NSAID must not be used
evidence_text: ### 4.3 When an NSAID must not be used Avoid oral NSAIDs in: chronic kidney disease or AKI (DG-03); anticoagulant therapy (DG-06); a history of gastrointestinal bleeding (DG-07); concurrent SSRI plus antiplatelet (section 3); heart failure; NSAID/aspirin hypersensitivity (ALG-003, MP-07). Where any applies, remain at step 2. PAT-009 (CKD G3b) was prescribed ibuprofen against this rule and developed AKI (INC-005, PR-07). PAT-006 (anticoagulated) used acetaminophen (PR-06). PAT-010 developed a bleed on ibuprofen with aspirin and sertraline (PR-07).

## 5. PRO-008: Renal Dose Adjustment (version 3, effective 2026-05-01) 1. Every inpatient order and every outpatient prescription for a drug in the MP-07 section 4.2 list is checked against the **most recent eGFR**. Pharmacy owns the check; Nephrology (DEP-005) advises. 2. **Metformin (FPA-03):** eGFR 45 or higher no cap; **eGFR 30 to 44 maximum 1,000 mg/day; eGFR below 30 stop** (MP-02, MP-07). 3. Other renal rules follow MP-07, including piperacillin-tazobactam (**3.375 g every 6 hours at eGFR 30 or below**), enoxaparin, lisinopril, spironolactone and apixaban. 4. A new eGFR that falls into a lower band triggers a **renal-dose alert**. In version 1 (to 2025-04-30) the alert went only to the pharmacist work queue; in **version 2 (2025-05-01 to 2026-04-30)** it also went to the prescriber's inbox; in **version 3 (from 2026-05-01)** it does both and in addition: - An **NSAID order (for example MED-026) at eGFR below 60 is a hard stop**; override requires a second pharmacist and a documented reason. 5. The metformin cap should be implemented within **14 days** of the qualifying eGFR. (PAT-001's cap was applied 21 days after the eGFR of 2025-02-20, during version 1 of this protocol, which routed the alert only to the pharmacist queue; PR-01.) 6. The change to version 3 followed INC-005 (PAT-009, ibuprofen prescribed 2026-03-05 with an overridden alert; PR-07, HO-08).

### 7.3 Antiplatelet choice Aspirin is the standard first antiplatelet in DG-06, but it is contraindicated for PAT-005 because of ALG-003. Clopidogrel was chosen as the documented alternative (DG-06, MP-03, MP-07).

### 3.5 SGLT2 inhibitor precautions SGLT2 inhibitors can cause ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose. The reference guideline requires: 1. Teach the **sick-day rule** at initiation: stop the drug during vomiting, fever, diarrhea, or poor oral intake, and for 3 days before elective surgery. 2. Check ketones if unwell even when glucose is not high. 3. After an episode of ketoacidosis attributed to an SGLT2 inhibitor, **do not re-challenge** with the drug class (MP-02). PAT-004 (PR-04) developed ketoacidosis on 2025-12-09 after not following the sick-day rule; empagliflozin was permanently stopped and recorded as an adverse drug reaction.

## 2. Purpose and Scope This chart records the care of PAT-004, who has type 2 diabetes (DIS-001) and hypothyroidism (DIS-016). It centers on an admission on 2025-12-09 for **diabetic ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose** (DIS-013) associated with the SGLT2 inhibitor empagliflozin (MED-030) during an acute febrile illness. The chart documents the ketone series, the insulin infusion and its transition criterion (FPA-12), a hypoglycemia alert during the infusion, and the permanent discontinuation of empagliflozin.

### 4.3 Potassium safety for mineralocorticoid antagonists Check potassium (LAB-005) and creatinine/eGFR (LAB-004) at **1 week and 4 weeks** after starting or increasing spironolactone. Do not increase the dose when potassium is above 5.0 mmol/L. Hold spironolactone and the ACE inhibitor if potassium reaches 5.5 mmol/L or higher; the management algorithm is in DG-03. The combination of MED-004 with MED-008 in CKD is a recognized hyperkalemia hazard (MP-06, MP-01); PAT-001 (PR-01) illustrates the monitoring schedule.

### 5.3 Application PAT-001 presented on 2025-09-17 with potassium 6.4 mmol/L and ECG changes after three days of vomiting and diarrhea during which the sick-day rule (DG-01) was not followed (PR-01). The telephone-notification delay for the result produced INC-002 (HO-08).

### 4.1 MediCore Heart-Failure Readmission Risk Score (fictional) One point each: admission for heart failure in the past 12 months; eGFR below 45; NT-proBNP above the age-band threshold at discharge (DG-01); atrial fibrillation; living alone; unreliable telephone contact. A score of **3 or more** triggers a nurse home-visit offer. PAT-011 scored 3 at the first discharge (atrial fibrillation, NT-proBNP 4,820 pg/mL, prior recent admission), which did not trigger an outreach because the score field was not completed.

### 4.5 After discharge Discharge after a heart-failure admission requires structured follow-up. The MediCore protocol is PRO-016 in HO-07, which sets a telephone call within 48 hours and a clinic visit within 7 days (FPA-06). Patients on warfarin (MED-013) also need an INR check within 72 hours of discharge under PRO-007 (HO-04). PAT-011 (PR-08) shows what happens when these steps fail.

### 4.3 Version 2 change (after INC-001) In **version 1 (to 2026-06-30)** the bar-code "urgent override" could bypass the nursing check if the prescriber documented urgency. In **version 2 (from 2026-07-01)** the override is a **hard stop**: the nursing check cannot be bypassed for a first beta-lactam dose in a patient with an allergy flag. The event that triggered the change is INC-001 (PAT-007, 2026-05-17; PR-07, HO-08).

### 5.4 Allergy documentation An allergy entry without verification, such as "rash, patient-reported, unverified," must not be treated as low risk. Before the first dose of a beta-lactam in any patient with an allergy flag, MediCore requires **dual verification** by pharmacist and nurse (PRO-003, FPA-09, HO-02). The failure of this step is the subject of INC-001 (HO-08).

### 3.1 Allergy flag before the event At registration in 2024-09 the patient reported a childhood rash to a penicillin. It was entered in the allergy field as "Penicillins: rash, patient-reported, unverified." The low severity and "unverified" status led staff to treat the flag as low risk.

### 6.1 Diagnosis ACS is diagnosed from symptoms, ECG (LAB-021), and hs-troponin (LAB-007). Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) requires a rise and/or fall of hs-troponin above the 99th percentile in the LD-01 range with ischemic symptoms or ECG change. Serial sampling at 0 and 2 hours is the MediCore standard (FPA-08; HO-03). ST-depression, as in PAT-002 and PAT-008, supports the diagnosis but is not required.

Antibiotics were escalated at 07:20: piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours (MED-018) plus vancomycin IV (MED-019) pending cultures. Ceftriaxone was discontinued.

evidence_text: ### 6.1 Emergency Department and sepsis bundle (PRO-004 version 2) On 2026-02-26 the sepsis bundle in force was **version 2** (first antibiotic within 60 minutes of the sepsis alert). Version 3, with a 50-minute target, took effect on 2026-03-01 (FPA-02; change record in HO-08). | Clock time (2026-02-26) | Event | |---|---| | 09:12 | Arrival at DEP-001 with three days of productive cough, fever, and worsening breathlessness | | 09:40 | Arterial blood gas (LAB-018) on room air: pH 7.28, PaCO2 8.3 kPa (62 mmHg), PaO2 7.7 kPa (58 mmHg) | | 09:55 | Chest X-ray (LAB-020): right lower lobe consolidation (report in LD-07) | | 10:05 | **Sepsis alert activated** (temperature 38.9 C, heart rate 124, respiratory rate 30, BP 96/58) | | 10:20 | Lactate (LAB-014) drawn: 3.4 mmol/L | | 10:25 | Blood cultures (LAB-012), two sets, drawn before antibiotics | | 10:58 | **First antibiotic: ceftriaxone 2 g IV (MED-017)**, 53 minutes after the alert | | 12:05 | Repeat lactate: 2.1 mmol/L (1 hour 45 minutes after the first; repeat required within 2 hours because the first value exceeded 2.5 mmol/L) | Compliance against version 2 (60 minutes): **met**. The same 53 minutes would **not** have met the version 3 target of 50 minutes. Inflammatory markers on arrival (LD-04): procalcitonin (LAB-015) 12.6 ng/mL; C-reactive protein (LAB-016) 214 mg/L. Treatment for the COPD exacerbation: prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days from 2026-02-26 (MED-023), albuterol nebulization every 4 hours, tiotropium continued, controlled oxygen with non-invasive ventilation overnight.

section: 2.2 Bundle elements (version 3; identical in version 2 except for the antibiotic target)
evidence_text: ### 2.2 Bundle elements (version 3; identical in version 2 except for the antibiotic target) 1. **Start event:** sepsis alert activated by the screening trigger (DG-05). 2. Measure lactate (LAB-014) at the alert; draw blood cultures (LAB-012) **before** the first antibiotic if this does not delay it. 3. **Give the first antibiotic within 50 minutes of the alert.** 4. Repeat lactate within **2 hours** if the first value is **above 2.5 mmol/L**. 5. Crystalloid resuscitation for hypotension or lactate of 4.0 mmol/L or higher. 6. Reassess and escalate through PRO-015 if mean arterial pressure stays below 65 mmHg. 7. Review cultures and de-escalate at 48 to 72 hours under PRO-013 (HO-04).

### 5.3 Application PAT-001 presented on 2025-09-17 with potassium 6.4 mmol/L and ECG changes after three days of vomiting and diarrhea during which the sick-day rule (DG-01) was not followed (PR-01). Spironolactone, lisinopril, furosemide and metformin were held; lisinopril restarted at 5 mg on 2025-09-26 and spironolactone resumed at 12.5 mg on 2025-10-23 with 1-week and 4-week potassium checks. The telephone-notification delay for the result produced INC-002 (HO-08).

### 4.3 Potassium safety for mineralocorticoid antagonists Check potassium (LAB-005) and creatinine/eGFR (LAB-004) at **1 week and 4 weeks** after starting or increasing spironolactone. Do not increase the dose when potassium is above 5.0 mmol/L. Hold spironolactone and the ACE inhibitor if potassium reaches 5.5 mmol/L or higher; the management algorithm is in DG-03. The combination of MED-004 with MED-008 in CKD is a recognized hyperkalemia hazard (MP-06, MP-01); PAT-001 (PR-01) illustrates the monitoring schedule.

### 4.3 The ACE-inhibitor decision DG-01 recommends a renin-angiotensin system blocker after ACS when LVEF is below 50% or hypertension persists. For PAT-008 the standard choice, an ACE inhibitor such as lisinopril (MED-004), is **contraindicated by ALG-004** (MP-01, MP-06, MP-07). MP-01 also advises caution with related receptor-blocking agents after ACE-inhibitor angioedema. No renin-angiotensin agent was started; blood pressure was addressed with metoprolol and cardiology re-review planned at 6 weeks (completed 2026-03-17, BP 132/80). Discharged 2026-02-07. Compare PAT-001 (PR-01), who takes lisinopril without any allergy flag.

section: 3.3 When an ACE inhibitor must not be used
evidence_text: ### 3.3 When an ACE inhibitor must not be used An ACE inhibitor is **contraindicated** after a previous episode of ACE-inhibitor-associated angioedema (ALG-004). Related receptor-blocking agents also require caution because angioedema can recur at a lower rate (MP-01, MP-06, MP-07). Example: PAT-008 (PR-07).

## 5. PRO-008: Renal Dose Adjustment (version 3, effective 2026-05-01) 1. Every inpatient order and every outpatient prescription for a drug in the MP-07 section 4.2 list is checked against the **most recent eGFR**. Pharmacy owns the check; Nephrology (DEP-005) advises. 2. **Metformin (FPA-03):** eGFR 45 or higher no cap; **eGFR 30 to 44 maximum 1,000 mg/day; eGFR below 30 stop** (MP-02, MP-07). 3. Other renal rules follow MP-07, including piperacillin-tazobactam (**3.375 g every 6 hours at eGFR 30 or below**), enoxaparin, lisinopril, spironolactone and apixaban. 4. A new eGFR that falls into a lower band triggers a **renal-dose alert**. In version 1 (to 2025-04-30) the alert went only to the pharmacist work queue; in **version 2 (2025-05-01 to 2026-04-30)** it also went to the prescriber's inbox; in **version 3 (from 2026-05-01)** it does both and in addition: - An **NSAID order (for example MED-026) at eGFR below 60 is a hard stop**; override requires a second pharmacist and a documented reason. 5. The metformin cap should be implemented within **14 days** of the qualifying eGFR. (PAT-001's cap was applied 21 days after the eGFR of 2025-02-20, during version 1 of this protocol, which routed the alert only to the pharmacist queue; PR-01.) 6. The change to version 3 followed INC-005 (PAT-009, ibuprofen prescribed 2026-03-05 with an overridden alert; PR-07, HO-08).

section: 4.3 When an NSAID must not be used
evidence_text: ### 4.3 When an NSAID must not be used Avoid oral NSAIDs in: chronic kidney disease or AKI (DG-03); anticoagulant therapy (DG-06); a history of gastrointestinal bleeding (DG-07); concurrent SSRI plus antiplatelet (section 3); heart failure; NSAID/aspirin hypersensitivity (ALG-003, MP-07). Where any applies, remain at step 2. PAT-009 (CKD G3b) was prescribed ibuprofen against this rule and developed AKI (INC-005, PR-07). PAT-006 (anticoagulated) used acetaminophen (PR-06). PAT-010 developed a bleed on ibuprofen with aspirin and sertraline (PR-07).

### 4.3 Causes and nephrotoxin avoidance Evaluate prerenal causes (volume depletion), renal causes (nephrotoxins, sepsis), and post-renal obstruction. Key nephrotoxin hazards in this dataset: - **NSAIDs with an ACE inhibitor and a diuretic**, the "triple combination," in a patient with CKD (PAT-009). - **Vancomycin with piperacillin-tazobactam** (MP-06, MP-04), requiring pharmacy-managed dosing and early level checks (PAT-013). - Dehydration during infection, with diuretics and ACE inhibitors continued.

### 6.1 Diagnosis ACS is diagnosed from symptoms, ECG (LAB-021), and hs-troponin (LAB-007). Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) requires a rise and/or fall of hs-troponin above the 99th percentile in the LD-01 range with ischemic symptoms or ECG change. Serial sampling at 0 and 2 hours is the MediCore standard (FPA-08; HO-03). ST-depression, as in PAT-002 and PAT-008, supports the diagnosis but is not required.

### 4.1 MediCore Heart-Failure Readmission Risk Score (fictional) One point each: admission for heart failure in the past 12 months; eGFR below 45; NT-proBNP above the age-band threshold at discharge (DG-01); atrial fibrillation; living alone; unreliable telephone contact. A score of **3 or more** triggers a nurse home-visit offer. PAT-011 scored 3 at the first discharge (atrial fibrillation, NT-proBNP 4,820 pg/mL, prior recent admission), which did not trigger an outreach because the score field was not completed.

### 4.5 After discharge Discharge after a heart-failure admission requires structured follow-up. The MediCore protocol is PRO-016 in HO-07, which sets a telephone call within 48 hours and a clinic visit within 7 days (FPA-06). Patients on warfarin (MED-013) also need an INR check within 72 hours of discharge under PRO-007 (HO-04). PAT-011 (PR-08) shows what happens when these steps fail.
